newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Tamil Tigers reject Sri Lanka call for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Tamil Tigers reject Sri Lanka call for peace talks.

text.p: The Tamil Tigers have rejected a conditional offer by Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga to resume peace talks to end the country's 13-year-old ethnic war, a Tamil separatist radio station said on Tuesday.

The Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) saw "nothing new" in the president's insistence that talks could be resumed only if the rebels indicate their willingness to lay down arms and agree to a fixed and limited time frame for the dialogue, said LTTE radio, monitored in northern Sri Lanka.

The latest exchange over the long-stalled peace talks took place as the Sri Lankan navy reported it had destroyed four LTTE boats and killed as many as 30 rebels on Monday near the northern city of Jaffna.
The Tiger rebels were preparing to mount suicide attacks on navy installations at Kankesanthurai harbour on the Jaffna peninsula, the navy said.
The LTTE, which often disputes government accounts of clashes, was not immediately available for comment.

In an interview with the state-owned Sunday Observer newspaper, Kumaratunga renewed the call for talks with the Tigers to end their war for an independent homeland in northern and eastern Sri Lanka. Talks were last held in early 1995.
Sri Lanka was open to the idea of third party mediation, the president said.
The two conditions were necessary because the Tigers had reneged on previous ceasefires and used the time to regroup and prepare for further hostilities, she said.
"We gave them almost everything they wanted, but they kicked us in the teeth," Kumaratunga said in the interview.
"Now it is clear that unless (LTTE chief Velupillai) Prabhakaran is so weakened that he has no other option, they are not likely to seriously enter into a dialogue," she said.
The government has mounted several major offensives against the rebels, capturing their northern Jaffna peninsula stronghold and confining the Tigers largely to jungle bases.
Defence spending this year has soared to almost 50 billion rupees ($877 million), compared with 32 billion rupees ($561 million) in 1995.

Colombo has said it wants to weaken the rebels militarily and force them back to the negotiating table in an effort to end the war, in which the government says more than 50,000 people have died. The LTTE says the toll is much higher.
On Monday a senior opposition lawmaker told a news conference the government's strategy was sending "conflicting signals" on the ethnic war.
"If you want peace, you have to prepare to negotiate with the LTTE," said Ronnie de Mel, a former finance minister and senior lawmaker from the opposition United National Party.
"One day you are going all out to finish off the LTTE...the next day (the president) comes and says 'I have not given up on the idea of negotiating with the LTTE.'"
